message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code (Title 2, Subtitle B). Here’s an overview of key rights you typically enjoy: | Category | Typical Tenant Rights | |----------|-----------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for residential units; two months for furnished units.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain premises in a safe, sanitary condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering your unit, except in emergencies. | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If landlord fails to repair major issues, you may withhold rent or pay repairs yourself and deduct from rent, but only if you follow proper procedures (written notice, time limits). | | **Discrimination** | • Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, etc. | | **Lease Terms** | • Written leases are not required for month‑to‑month agreements, but it’s advisable to have one.
• Lease terms cannot violate public policy or be unconscionable. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For nonpayment of rent: 3‑day written notice to cure.
• For termination of tenancy: 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month; 60 days for longer leases. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a valid notice (e.g., 3‑day notice to pay rent or quit).
• Eviction requires filing a lawsuit; self‑eviction or “no‑court” eviction is illegal. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws; rent increases are governed by lease terms or local ordinances. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must keep utilities operational unless otherwise specified in lease. | ### Practical Steps If You’re Facing Issues 1. **Document Everything** – Keep records of communications, photos of problems, receipts for repairs, etc. 2. **Written Notice** – Send a certified letter or email to the landlord detailing the issue and requesting repair. 3. **Follow Up** – If the landlord doesn’t act within a reasonable timeframe (often 7–10 days for major repairs), you may consider withholding rent or repairing yourself. 4. **Seek Mediation** – Many counties offer free mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. 5. **Legal Aid** – If costs become prohibitive, look into local legal aid organizations that specialize in housing law. If you need a more detailed explanation tailored to a particular situation (e.g., a specific lease clause or dispute), let me know!
